name: ADUM3151ARSZ
title: 3.75 kV seven-channel SPI digital isolators, ADuM3151, ADuM3152 and ADuM3153
summary: Seven-channel transformer-coupled (iCoupler) digital isolators laid out for an isolated SPI port. Four fast channels carry clock, MOSI and slave select from the master side and MISO back, at up to 17 MHz SPI clock in the B grade or 1 MHz in the glitch-filtered A grade. Three further slow channels, sampled and passed at 250 kbps, run in a direction set by the model: ADuM3151 two forward and one back, ADuM3152 one forward and two back, ADuM3153 all three back. Each side runs from its own 3.0 V to 5.5 V supply; the barrier is rated 3750 V rms for 1 minute in a 20-lead SSOP with 5.1 mm creepage.
key_figures: 4 fast SPI (CLK, MO/SI, SS forward; MI/SO back) + 3 slow
1 MHz max (A grade); 17 MHz max (B grade, 5 V)
25 ns max (A); 14 ns max, 12 ns typ (B)
250 kbps; delay 0.1 µs to 2.6 µs; jitter 2.5 µs

operation.text: All three models share the fast channels: MCLK to SCLK, MO to SI and MSS to SSS cross from side 1 to side 2, and SO crosses back to MI. They differ only in the three slow channels: the ADuM3151 sends A and B from side 1 and C from side 2; the ADuM3152 sends A from side 1 and B and C from side 2; the ADuM3153 sends all three from side 2 to side 1.

In the A grade the clock, MO/SI and MI/SO channels have a glitch filter, which adds delay and gives high noise immunity. The B grade leaves it out of those three for low delay: 14 ns maximum, allowing a 17 MHz clock in ordinary 4-wire SPI. In the B grade a glitch shorter than 10 ns can lose its second edge, giving a false output transition that lasts until a refresh or the next real edge, so such glitches must be kept off its inputs; the A grade is the choice for noisy surroundings. The SS channel has the glitch filter in both grades because many uses of slave select act on its edges; in the B grade MSS needs 10 ns setup before the first active clock edge to cover the filter's extra delay.

The channels do not lock to the clock, so any SPI mode, clock polarity or clock-to-data timing passes. Clock and MOSI paths are tuned for delay and for matching between channels; the MISO path for delay alone. MI is always driven and does not go to high impedance when slave select is inactive, so several MI lines cannot share a wire without a tristate buffer or multiplexer.

The levels of every input on one side, fast and slow, are sampled together by a free-running internal clock, packed and sent across one coil; the far side checks the fast channels' DC levels and drives the slow outputs, then the process runs the other way. Because inputs are sampled at discrete times, a slow channel's delay is anywhere from 0.1 µs to 2.6 µs depending on where the edge falls against the sample clock. Two edges on same-direction slow channels that fall between samples come out together; a very small gap between edges is stretched to one output clock period; a pulse shorter than the minimum slow pulse width can be missed. Edges separated by at least tVIx SKEW keep their order.

Each input edge sends a pulse of about 1 ns through the transformer to set or reset a bistable decoder. If the input has not changed for more than about 1.2 µs, refresh pulses carrying the present level are sent over the slow channel. If the slow decoder receives nothing for more than about 5 µs, a watchdog takes the input side to be unpowered or faulty and puts the output into high impedance.
With either supply off, the outputs on both sides, SSS included, are high impedance; outputs on the unpowered side sit no more than a diode drop above ground.

The transformer output pulses exceed 1.5 V and the decoder senses at about 1.0 V, leaving a 0.5 V margin for induced voltage. The allowable field is set so the induced voltage is no more than half that margin, at 3 V operation, the most susceptible case. At 1 MHz the allowable field is 0.5 kgauss, which induces 0.25 V at the receiving coil; at worst-case polarity during a transmitted pulse this cuts the received pulse from more than 1.0 V to 0.75 V, still above the 0.5 V sensing threshold. External fields matter only for currents of great size and high frequency flowing next to the part: at 1 MHz it takes a 1.2 kA current 5 mm away to affect operation. In strong high-frequency fields, loops in board traces can induce enough voltage to trip the following circuits, so loop-forming layouts are to be avoided.

The logic pins need no external interface parts. Both VDD1 and VDD2 need a bypass capacitor of 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF, with the total lead length between the capacitor ends and the supply pin no more than 20 mm; the recommended layout places it within 2 mm. Where common-mode transients are high, coupling across the barrier on the board is to be kept small and laid out so it reaches all pins on one side equally; otherwise pin-to-pin differences can exceed the absolute maximum ratings and cause latch-up or damage.

Propagation delay is input 50% to output 50%, and can differ between falling (tPHL) and rising (tPLH) edges. Pulse width distortion is the largest difference between those two delays. Channel-to-channel matching is the largest difference in delay between channels of one part.

Supply current on a channel depends on supply voltage, data rate, output load and whether the channel is fast or slow. The slow channels draw a fixed quiescent current from their internal back-and-forth data path; their capacitive load losses are negligible beside it, so they appear only as IDD1(Q) and IDD2(Q). The fast channels' dynamic current adds to that. The total supply current curves are taken with all fast channels at the same rate and the slow channels idle.

Insulation degrades by surface tracking, which sets creepage in system standards and depends on working voltage, environment and material group, and by wear-out, driven by displacement current in the polyimide. DC stress causes very little wear-out; the AC part of the voltage causes it. The working voltage for wear-out can differ from that for tracking, and most standards specify the tracking one. The DC limit in the working voltage table comes from package creepage per IEC 60664-1 and can differ under particular system standards.
